Appearance:
Shri Santosh Agrawal- learned counsel and Smt. Padamshri Agrawal- learned counsel for the petitioner.
Shri K.S. Tomar- learned Government Advocate for the respondents/State.
Reserved on : 05/02/2026  Delivered on : 17/02/2026  ORDER 1.

The petitioner has filed this writ petition challenging the order, dated 26.07.2022, (Annexure P-1)
whereby punishment of recovery of Rs.4,82,423/- has been imposed upon the petitioner.
He has been also imposed with the punishment of censure.
2. The petitioner, during the period from 29.09.2015 to 30.11.2020, was posted as Range Assistant in Seondha Range, Forest Division, Datia.

In relation to certain illegal excavation of the minerals, a charge- sheet under Rule 16 of The M.P. Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1966 was issued to the petitioner on 28.11.2020 (Annexure P-3).

entities.text: M.P. Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1966
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The petitioner gave detailed reply to this charge-sheet on 21.10.2021 (Annexure P-4) and, thereafter, the respondents have passed the impugned order on 25.07.2022, whereby the petitioner was found guilty of dereliction of duty, as a result of which loss of Rs.4,82,423/- was caused to the Government, which has been directed to be recovered from the petitioner.
He was also censured.
Challenging this order, the petitioner has filed the present writ petition.
3. The learned counsel for the petitioner challenged the impugned order of punishment on two grounds.

Firstly, he submitted that since the petitioner raised disputed question of facts in his reply,
a detailed departmental enquiry ought to have been conducted by the respondents under Rule 14 of CCA Rules.
Counsel for the petitioner placed reliance upon the Apex Court judgment in the case of O.K. Bharadwaj Vs. Union of India & others reported in (2001)9 SCC 180.

entities.text: O.K. Bharadwaj Vs. Union of India & others reported in (2001)9 SCC 180
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Secondly, he submitted that since the petitioner had already retired on 30.09.2020, the punishment order could not have been passed without the approval of the Governor in view of provisions of Rule 9 of M.P. Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1976.
The learned counsel for the petitioner also challenged the finding recorded against him in the impugned order on merits.
He, therefore, prayed for setting aside the Dayal Singh Parihar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 17 February, 2026

4. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondents supported the impugned order and submitted that admittedly during the period from 29.09.2015 to 30.11.2020, the petitioner was posted as Range Assistant in Seondha Range, Forest Division, Datia, wherein illegal excavation of minerals were found.

He further submitted that the petitioner has not disputed the fact that he was responsible for the safety and security of the forest range and, therefore, since the loss is caused to the Government during the period of his posting, he has been rightly imposed with the punishment of recovery of the amount of loss caused to the Government.
He further submitted that the respondent Divisional Forest Officer was competent to impose punishment upon the petitioner.

5. Considered the arguments and perused the record.
6.

Firstly, the ground raised by the counsel for the petitioner with regard to conduct of the detailed enquiry under Rule 14 of the the M.P. Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1966 needs to be considered.

entities.text: M.P. Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1966
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 7. The Rule 16 of the CCA Rules provides for procedure for imposing minor penalties.

entities.text: Dayal Singh Parihar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, under clause (b) of Rule 16(1), the disciplinary authority has been given liberty to form an opinion as to whether enquiry as contemplated under Rule 14 is required in the facts and circumstances of the case or not?

9. Pari materia provisions of Regulation 16 of the Food Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations,
1971 were under considered by the Apex Court in the case of the Food Corporation of India,
Hyderabad & others Vs. Prahalada Rao & another reported in (2001)1 SCC 165 wherein the Court held in para 5 as under:-
"5.

entities.text:
Food Corporation of India,
Hyderabad & others Vs. Prahalada Rao & another reported in (2001)1 SCC 165
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In our view, on the basis of the allegation that Food Corporation of India is misusing its power of imposing minor penalties, the Regulation cannot be interpreted contrary to its language.
Regulation 60(1)(b) mandates the disciplinary authority to form its opinion whether it is necessary to hold inquiry in a particular case or not.
But that would not mean that in all cases where an employee disputes his liability, a full-fledged inquiry should be held.
Otherwise, the entire purpose of incorporating summary procedure for imposing minor penalties would be frustrated.
If the discretion given under Regulation 60(1)(b) is misused or is exercised in an arbitrary manner, it is open to the employee to challenge the same before the appropriate forum.
It is for the disciplinary authority to decide whether regular departmental enquiry as contemplated under Regulation 58 for imposing major penalty should be followed or not.
This discretion cannot be curtailed by interpretation which is contrary to the language used.

Further, Regulation 60(2) itself provides that in a case if it is proposed to withhold increments of pay and such withholding of increments is likely to affect adversely the amount of retirement benefits payable to an employee and in such other cases as mentioned therein, the disciplinary authority shall hold inquiry in the manner laid down in Regulation 58 before making any order imposing any such penalty.

Hence, it is apparent that the High Court erroneously interpreted the Regulation by holding that once the employee denies the charge, it is incumbent upon the authority to conduct inquiry contemplated for imposing major penalty.
It also erred in holding that where an employee denies that loss is caused to the Corporation either by his negligence or breach of order, such inquiry should be held.

It is settled law that court's power of judicial review in such cases is limited and court can interfere where the authority held the inquiry proceedings in a manner inconsistent with the rules of natural justice or in violation of statutory rules prescribing the mode of inquiry and imposing punishment or where the conclusion or finding reached by the disciplinary authority is based on no evidence or is such that no reasonable person would have ever reached.

As per the Regulation, holding of Dayal Singh Parihar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 17 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199916415/
3 regular departmental enquiry is a discretionary power of the disciplinary authority which is to be exercised by considering the facts of each case and if it is misused or used arbitrarily, it would be subject to judicial review."

10. Learned counsel for the petitioner relied upon judgment of the Apex Court in the case of O.K.
Bhardwaj (supra) to say that full fledged departmental enquiry ought to have been conducted.

The judgments rendered in the case of O.K. Bhardwaj and FCI (supra) have been reconciled by the Division Bench of this Court in the case of Union of India & another Vs. C.P. Singh reported in 2004(2) MPJR 252 (= 2004 SCC Online MP 811).

entities.text: Union of India & another Vs. C.P. Singh reported in 2004(2) MPJR 252 (= 2004 SCC Online MP 811)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Court held as under:-
"Position after decision in FCI: Where the Rules give a discretion to the Disciplinary Authority to either hold a summary enquiry or regular enquiry, it is not possible to say that the Disciplinary Authority should direct only a regular enquiry, when an employee denies the charge or requests for an inquiry.

Even in such cases, the Disciplinary Authority has the discretion to decide, for reasons to be recorded,
whether a regular enquiry should be held or not.

If he decides not to hold a regular enquiry and proceeds to decide the matter summarily, the employee can always challenge the minor punishment imposed, on the ground that the decision not to hold a regular enquiry was an arbitrary decision.
In that event, the Court or Tribunal will in exercise of power of judicial review, examine whether the decision of the Disciplinary Authority not to hold an enquiry was arbitrary.
If the Court/Tribunal holds that the decision was arbitrary, then such decision not to hold an enquiry and the consequential imposition of punishment will be quashed.
If the Court/Tribunal holds that the decision was not arbitrary, then the imposition of minor penalty will stand.

It is also possible to read the decisions in Bharadwaj and FCI harmoniously, if Bharadwaj is read as stating a general principle, without reference to any specific rules, that it is incumbent upon the Disciplinary Authority to hold a regular enquiry,
even for imposing a minor penalty, if the charge is factual and the charge is denied by the employee.

On the other hand, the decision in FCI holding that the Disciplinary Authority has the discretion to dispense with a regular enquiry, even where the charge is factual and the employee denies the charge, is with reference to the specific provisions of a Rule vesting such discretion."
11. Thus, in view of the discretion conferred on the disciplinary authority under Rule 16, a regular departmental enquiry can be dispensed with depending upon the facts of the case.

However, if the authority decides not to hold a regular enquiry and proceeds to decide the matter summarily, such a decision is open to judicial review by this Court.
12.
In view of the aforesaid legal position, the facts of the present case needs to be considered.
13. The petitioner was working as Range Assistant in Seondha Range, Forest Division, District- Datia.

On a complaint made, an inspection was made by the Flying Squad of Room No.P-12, P-13 &

sentences.text: The inspection was made in presence of the petitioner.
During inspection about 10 pits were found in Room No.13 which were 7 to 8 months old.
The measurement of pits was taken by GPS reading, the photographs were taken and a Panchnama was prepared which was duly signed by the petitioner.
As per the measurement, about 2352.73 cubic meter bolder was found extracted.
Another inspection made by the Flying Squad on 20/21.02.2020 of the same area, 11 new pits were found of which the measurement was taken through GPS reading and a Panchnama was prepared.
14. Based upon the aforesaid total 2363 cubic meter boulders are found extracted amounting Rs.14,13,507/- the petitioner's accountability has been apportioned to 1/3rd of the total amount.
Accordingly, he been directed to deposit Rs.4,24,051/-.
The censure is also imposed on him.
15. At the outset, it be noted that the petitioner had an alternate remedy of filing an appeal against the punishment order.
Needless to mention, appellate authority was well equipped with power to appreciate the factual aspects of the matter also.
However, the petitioner chose not to avail the alternative remedy of filing an appeal.
It is settled that in exercise of powers of judicial review, this Court can examine the decision making process only.
Thus, findings as recorded in the impugned order are not open to interference in power of judicial review so long as there is some material to support such finding.
So far as the process adopted by the respondents, the same is found to be proper inasmuch as the petitioner was given a show-cause notice to which he submitted his reply.
The reply given by him is duly considered by the authority.
The reasons have been assigned in the impugned order based upon the material collected during the inspection in presence of the petitioner.
Thus, the requirement of Rule 16 of CCA Rules as also that of principles of natural justice have been satisfied.
The impugned order passed by respondent authority is thus found to be just and proper.
16. On the date, of the impugned order was passed on 25.07.2022, the petitioner had already retired.

Learned counsel for the petitioner, therefore, raised an objection regarding validity of the impugned order inasmuch as the sanction from the Governor of the State was not obtained as is required under Rule 9 of the Pension Rules.

17. Rule 9 of the Pension Rules provides as under:
"9. Right of governor to withhold or withdraw pension.-(1) The Governor reserves to himself the right of withholding or withdrawing a pension or part thereof, whether permanently or for a specified period, and of ordering recovery from pension of the whole or part of any pecuniary loss caused to the Government if, in any departmental or judicial proceeding, the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct or negligence during the period of his service, including service rendered upon re- employment after retirement:
Provided that the State Public Service Commission shall be con-sulted before any final orders are passed:

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199916415/
5

Provided further that where a part of pension is withheld or withdrawn, the amount of such pension shall not be reduced below Ithe minimum pension as determined by the Government from time to time:
(2) (a) The departmental proceedings 2[x x x), if instituted while the Government servant was in service whether before his retirement or during his re-employment,
shall, after the final retirement of the Government servant, be deemed to be proceedings under this rule and shall be continued an concluded by the authority by which they were commenced, in the same manner as if the Government servant had continued in service:
Provided that where the departmental proceedings are instituted by an authority subordinate to the Governor, that authority shall submit a report regarding its findings to the Governor."
18. Thus, by virtue of proviso to Rule 9(2)(a), the authority was required to submit regarding its finding to the Governor and thereafter order could have been passed by the Governor.
The learned counsel for the respondents could not point out that the impugned order is passed by the Governor or the matter was ever referred to Governor.
Thus, the impugned order, dated 26.07.2022 (Annexure-P/1) is found to have been passed in violation of Rule 9 of the Pension Rules.
Accordingly, upholding the findings recorded in the impugned order, the same is set- aside for want of competence on the part of the respondent/Divisional Forest Officer.
19. The respondents are, however, given liberty to pass a fresh order in accordance with Rule 9 of the Pension Rules.
Let the same be done within a period of 90 days' from the date of submission of the certified copy of this order.
20. With the aforesaid, this writ petition is disposed off.
(ASHISH SHROTI)
